name: JDBC URL parts
desc: The URL selects the driver, names the server and the schema, and carries driver options. Credentials belong in getConnection, not in the URL.
body:
Read the URL right to left. The database name is the last path segment, the host and port come before it, and the subprotocol right after `jdbc:` decides which driver answers. A missing or misspelled subprotocol gives `No suitable driver found` even when the jar sits on the classpath.

Options after the `?` are driver specific. `serverTimezone=UTC` stops Connector/J 8 from shifting timestamps, and `rewriteBatchedStatements=true` turns a batch of inserts into multi-row statements. `useSSL=false` is acceptable only for a local exam database.

Keep the password out of the URL. URLs are printed by `getMetaData().getURL()`, written to logs, and captured in shell history.

name: setTransactionIsolation
desc: Sets the isolation level for the connection. It applies to the next transaction, so call it before setAutoCommit(false) or before the first statement commits.
body:
The level decides which concurrency problems are possible. `READ_UNCOMMITTED` allows dirty reads, `READ_COMMITTED` stops them, `REPEATABLE_READ` keeps a row stable inside the transaction, and `SERIALIZABLE` makes the result equivalent to running the transactions one after another. Higher levels mean more locking and more deadlocks.

Changing the level in the middle of a transaction is implementation defined. MySQL applies it to the next transaction, so the current one keeps its old level and the code looks correct while doing something else.

Pools keep the level they were configured with. If a method lowers it, put it back in `finally` the same way you restore `autoCommit`.

name: Savepoint
desc: Marks a point inside a transaction. Rolling back to it undoes only the later statements and leaves the transaction open for more work.
body:
A savepoint is the tool for an all-or-nothing sub-step. One example is an audit row that may be rejected by a constraint, while the main booking must still commit. A full rollback would throw away the booking too.

Call `rollback(sp)` rather than `rollback()`. The no-argument form ends the whole transaction and releases every savepoint in it.

After a rollback to a savepoint, that savepoint may be considered used up by the driver, so keep `releaseSavepoint` on the success path only. MySQL supports savepoints on InnoDB and ignores them on MyISAM, which never rolls anything back.

name: setNull
desc: Binds a real SQL NULL with an explicit type. More portable than setString(index, null), which some drivers reject or send as an empty string.
body:
`setString(index, null)` happens to work with Connector/J because the driver translates it, but the JDBC specification does not require that. `setNull` states the type, so the driver can prepare the parameter without guessing.

An untyped `Types.NULL` is accepted by some drivers and rejected by others when the column type cannot be inferred. Name the real column type and the problem disappears.

The distinction matters for queries. `WHERE description IS NULL` finds a `setNull` row, while `WHERE description = ''` finds an empty string. Both look the same in a Java object where the field is null, so decide at the write side which one you mean.

name: ResultSet.wasNull()
desc: Reports whether the last column read was SQL NULL. Required whenever a primitive getter turns NULL into 0, false, or 0.0.
body:
`wasNull` is a property of the last getter call on that result set, not of the column. Calling `getString` after `getInt` replaces the flag, so the check has to sit on the line after the read it belongs to.

The alternative is to skip the primitive getter entirely: `(Integer) rs.getObject("stars")` returns null for a NULL column and the boxed value otherwise. That is shorter, and it costs one cast.

A zero that really means zero is the dangerous case. A hotel with zero stars and a hotel with no rating produce the same int, and only `wasNull` tells them apart.

name: Generated keys by column
desc: Asks for named generated columns instead of every generated column. Useful when a table has more than one auto-generated or defaulted column.
body:
Both forms reach the same driver call. `RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS` asks for all generated columns, while the string array asks for the named ones. With one auto-increment column the difference is invisible, and with a table that also has a generated timestamp it matters.

The returned result set has one row and one column per requested key for an insert. For a batch, the driver usually returns one row per statement, but the order is not guaranteed by the specification. Do not zip the key rows against your input list unless the driver documents it.

Read with `getInt(1)` in an exam answer. Column labels in the key result set are driver specific, so a name that works with Connector/J may fail with another driver.

name: setFetchSize
desc: Hints how many rows the driver should retrieve per round trip. A hint only, and some drivers ignore it without streaming enabled.
body:
Fetch size trades memory for round trips. A large value means fewer network waits and more rows held in the driver. A small value keeps memory flat and costs more trips. A few hundred is a normal starting point for a report.

MySQL's default behaviour is to read the whole result set into memory before `executeQuery` returns. Real streaming needs `setFetchSize(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` with Connector/J, or `useCursorFetch=true` plus a positive fetch size. Without one of those, the call is accepted and ignored.

A streaming result set holds the connection open until it is closed. Reading a million rows and then running another statement on the same connection fails or blocks, so keep the streaming read on its own connection.

name: setQueryTimeout
desc: Limits how long a statement may run, in seconds. The driver cancels it and throws SQLTimeoutException when the limit passes.
body:
The timeout is implemented as a cancel request from the driver, so the server has to support cancellation. MySQL does, through a second connection that sends `KILL QUERY`. The cancel itself can fail, in which case the original statement keeps running and the exception says why.

Five seconds is generous for an indexed lookup and far too long for a health check. Set the value per statement, not once for the whole application, because a report and a login query have different budgets.

A timeout is not a substitute for an index. A query that times out under load usually needs a better plan, not a longer limit.

name: DatabaseMetaData.getTables
desc: Lists tables as a normal ResultSet. The catalog is the schema name in MySQL and null in SQLite; the types array filters out views.
body:
The four arguments are catalog, schema pattern, table pattern, and types. `null` means no filter for any of them, and `%` is the SQL wildcard. Passing `new String[]{"TABLE"}` excludes views, which otherwise show up next to real tables.

The catalog argument confuses people who come from PostgreSQL. In MySQL the catalog is the database, so `conn.getCatalog()` is the right value and the schema argument stays null. In PostgreSQL it is the other way around. Passing the database name as the schema argument returns zero rows and looks like a missing table.

These calls return ordinary result sets. Close them, and remember that the pattern comparison follows the server's collation, which is case sensitive for table names on Linux MySQL.

name: clearBatch
desc: Drops the accumulated parameter sets without executing them. Call it after each executeBatch so a long input does not grow driver memory.
body:
Without `clearBatch`, the driver keeps every parameter set until the statement is closed. A loop over a million rows then holds a million parameter arrays, and the memory win from batching disappears. After `executeBatch` the sets are executed but not necessarily discarded.

The chunk size is a compromise. Each `executeBatch` is one round trip, so 500 rows per trip is fine and 50 rows is wasteful. Above a few thousand, a failure means retrying a large unit and the driver's packet limit can be reached.

`executeBatch` returns one count per statement. `Statement.SUCCESS_NO_INFO` (-2) means the driver executed the statement but will not report a count, which is normal for some drivers and is not an error.

name: SQLException details
desc: SQLState is the standard five character code, the error code is vendor specific, and the chained next exception carries the rest of the batch failures.
body:
`SQLState` comes from the SQL standard and is the portable part. `08` means connection failure, `23` integrity violation, `28` invalid authorization, `42` syntax or missing object, and `40` deadlock or timeout. `getErrorCode()` is whatever the vendor returned and means nothing on another database.

`42S02` from MySQL means a missing table, `42S22` a missing column. Those two cover most first-run failures, and both are in the message as well, so read it before adding logging.

Subclasses carry meaning: `SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException` is recoverable by showing a duplicate message, `SQLTimeoutException` is worth a retry, and `SQLTransientConnectionException` suggests a pool problem. Catch the subclass you can act on and let the rest escape.

Always pass the original exception as the cause when you translate. Losing it removes the SQLState from every log line above the repository.

name: setObject with a type
desc: Binds a value with an explicit SQL type. Use it for LocalDate and BigDecimal, or when the driver would guess a type the column does not accept.
body:
`setObject(index, value)` lets the driver infer the SQL type from the Java class. That works for `String` and `Integer` and is risky for dates, because `LocalDate` can be sent as `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`, or a string depending on the driver version. Passing `Types.DATE` explicitly removes the guess.

On the read side the mirror call is `rs.getObject("start_date", LocalDate.class)`. Both directions need JDBC 4.2 and a driver that implements it. Connector/J 8 does; an old 5.x jar does not.

When an exam answer has to work anywhere, use `java.sql.Date.valueOf(localDate)` and `rs.getDate(...).toLocalDate()`. It is two conversions longer and it never depends on driver behaviour.
